name: Hilton's Law
statement: The nerve supplying a joint also supplies the muscles that move the joint and the skin over them.
statementAccent: also supplies the muscles that move the joint
meaning: The articular nerves of a joint are branches of the same nerve trunks that innervate the muscles crossing and moving that joint, and those trunks also supply the skin overlying those muscles. This ties together the sensory and motor innervation of a joint, its movers, and its overlying skin into one shared nerve supply.
mechanism: The shared innervation reflects common developmental origin of the joint, its muscles, and the overlying skin from related segments. Because the same nerve carries pain from the joint and controls the muscles around it, joint irritation can trigger protective reflex muscle spasm and can refer pain to the overlying skin.

examples.text: The knee is supplied by branches of the femoral, obturator, and sciatic nerves, all of which also supply muscles that move the knee.
The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the coracobrachialis, biceps, and brachialis, the elbow joint, and the overlying forearm skin.
The obturator nerve supplies both hip and knee, explaining why hip pathology can refer pain to the knee.

whyItMatters: It lets clinicians and anatomists predict a joint's sensory supply from the muscles that move it, and it explains referred pain and protective muscle spasm around an injured joint. This guides examination, regional anesthesia, and interpretation of pain patterns.
limits: It is an anatomical generalization rather than an exact rule, and individual variation exists. Not every articular nerve fits neatly, and the relationship is best treated as a strong tendency describing correlation of supply, not a mechanistic guarantee.
misreadings: It is sometimes read as claiming a single nerve supplies each joint, whereas most joints receive branches from several nerves that also move that joint.
origin: John Hilton, British surgeon (1805–1878), in lectures delivered 1860–1862 and published as "On Rest and Pain" (1863).

sources.text: Wikipedia's article on Hilton's law, stating the nerve-joint-muscle-skin principle and its origin in Hilton's 1860–1862 lectures — supports the statement, attribution, and examples.
Encyclopaedia Britannica's entry on Hilton's law, defining the nerve-joint-muscle-skin relationship — supports the statement of the law.
